subject: people with medical aid who still pay extra out of their own pocket: co-payments, savings running out, preferred pharmacies and doubts about generics
citation: Mpanza NM, Bradley H, Laing R (2019). Reasons why insured consumers co-pay for medicines at retail pharmacies in Pretoria, South Africa. Afr J Prim Health Care Fam Med 11(1):a1878. doi:10.4102/phcfm.v11i1.1878

claims.text: Co-payments are confusing and unexplained, so an unexplained charge gets accepted or paid under confusion rather than questioned
evaluative_rules: Treat an unexplained charge as something to accept and pay, not something to interrogate
objections: Why am I paying extra when I already pay monthly?

readings.text: Someone who has seen the same medicine suddenly require a co-payment a month later would weigh any new charge with suspicion, but without a clear way to calculate it they may still accept it rather than question it.

If someone has tried to get an explanation from the schemes offices and found them useless, they would approach a new charge expecting the explanation to be unhelpful and would be less likely to ask again.

Someone who has heard explanations about thresholds and gaps but still does not understand them would weigh a new charge as just another part of a system they cannot follow, making them less likely to challenge it.

If someone is already upset because they are sick and just wants to get their medication and leave, they would weigh a new charge as something to pay quickly to avoid more upset, even if they do not understand it.

claims.text: Day-to-day benefits run through a savings account that depletes, so a purchase is judged by whether it draws on remaining savings or triggers out-of-pocket payment
evaluative_rules: Judge a medicine by whether savings still cover it or an outstanding amount falls to you
objections: Will this come out of my savings or will I have to co-pay?

readings.text: Someone who judges a purchase by whether it draws on remaining savings or triggers out-of-pocket payment would weigh a new product by whether it fits within the savings account balance before it runs out.

If a purchase is judged by whether it draws on remaining savings or triggers out-of-pocket payment, a new product would be weighed by whether it is covered under the day-to-day benefits funded from savings accounts.
Someone who hardly experiences a co-payment because the scheme pays from a savings account would weigh a new product by whether it can be paid from that account rather than as an outstanding amount.

If day-to-day benefits are funded from savings accounts for the majority of schemes, a new product would be weighed by whether it falls under those savings-funded day-to-day benefits or under hospicentric specialist benefits.

claims.text: Scheme-designated or corporate pharmacies are the appropriate place to fill prescriptions, so availability at the preferred pharmacy decides the purchase
evaluative_rules: Judge a pharmacy by whether the scheme prefers it or it reliably stocks the prescription
objections: Is this available at the pharmacy my scheme told me to use?

readings.text: Someone who only co-pays at big corporate pharmacies because their medical scheme prefers them would weigh a new pharmacy option by whether their scheme designates it, not by its co-pay amount.
If a person assumes corporate pharmacies will always have the prescription, they would be less open to a new service that relies on small pharmacies with limited stock capabilities.
Someone who fears a small pharmacy will give an alternative medicine not prescribed by the doctor would weigh a new option mainly on whether it guarantees the exact prescribed medicine.
If a person was told by their scheme to go to big corporate pharmacies, they might still consider a new option if it is presented as scheme-designated, even if they currently co-pay there.

claims.text: Generics are suspected of being inferior, weaker, slower, or impure because they are made by tweaking the manufacturing process
evaluative_rules: Judge a medicine by originator quality, not by price
objections: Is this generic as good as the original?

readings.text: Someone who questions whether generics are inferior or weak would weigh a new product by first asking whether it is of the same quality as originators, not by assuming it is equivalent.
Someone who thinks generics take much longer to work would weigh a new product by expecting it to be slower to show results than an originator, even if it is presented as the same thing.

Someone who assumes a generic is made by tweaking the process of developing the medicine would weigh a new product by wondering what reactants were used and whether there are impurities, rather than trusting that it is identical.

If someone assumes the doctor knows about possible impurities, they would weigh a new product by deferring to a doctor's judgement about whether it is safe or pure enough, rather than deciding on their own.

claims.text: A familiar pharmacist is a caring, reliable advisor because doctors may be guessing, so the pharmacist's recommendation or established relationship decides the purchase
evaluative_rules: Trust a pharmacist who knows you and your family over an unfamiliar one

readings.text: Someone who relies on their pharmacy for a second opinion because doctors are guessing sometimes would weigh a new service by whether it preserves that pharmacist's role as a caring, reliable advisor.
If a pharmacist's established relationship decides the purchase, a new product would be weighed by how easily the familiar pharmacist can explain and stand behind it.
Someone who travels to their old pharmacy because they care about you and discuss stuff with them would be cautious about a new option that might bypass that relationship.
If the pharmacist's recommendation decides the purchase, a new policy would be weighed by whether it still lets the pharmacist give a second opinion when the doctor seems to be guessing.

confidence: qualitative interviews, single urban region, fieldwork year not specified — mechanisms durable, magnitudes unknown
year_note: Published 2019; the paper does not state the fieldwork dates.
